steps.title: Trace one displayed object to a source
steps.explanation: The humerus label links to the original FJ3368 OBJ, with its SHA-256 and topology counts. The displayed metre coordinates come from division of source millimetres by 1,000 and a view rotation. Hash identity checks bytes, not anatomical correctness.
steps.observe: The humerus record exposes 2,233 vertices, 3,784 triangles and its source hash. Original notices are retained.

steps.title: Repeat the check on another component
steps.explanation: Select brachialis and confirm that its name, OBJ and hash change independently. This prevents an assembly-level citation from obscuring which component is actually displayed. Source licensing and the scope of a numerical claim remain separate records.
steps.observe: The record changes to FJ1486: 1,266 vertices and 1,746 triangles. No muscle force, fitted modulus or proof of contact accuracy is attached to this surface.

steps.title: Keep attribution and scientific support separate
steps.explanation: Restore the atlas and follow the chapter’s component licences, transformation record and primary references. BodyParts3D’s current CC BY 4.0 record coexists with retained historical OBJ notices; Kenoma’s code licence does not relicense those assets. Lean cards below identify their own exact mathematical assumptions.
steps.observe: All ten parts retain their own provenance. Source identity, licence, geometry checks and mathematical proof do not become clinical validation.

audit.finding: Surface picking alone and a generic source link made component identity difficult to inspect and blurred citation with scientific validation.
audit.change: Named component selections and repeated source/count checks teach provenance independently of constitutive or proof claims.
audit.remaining: No new asset licence, source download, biological validation or mathematical theorem is introduced; existing source and proof receipts remain authoritative.
